raw: {"patients": "Live rats (~10-20?) bred, shipped, housed five weeks in a homeschool setting, then killed — the only patients whose sentient experience is shaped by Marisa's choices, since they're alive during the unit. Frogs: many biological supply frogs are wild-caught (Rana pipiens especially), so the order can drive removal from declining wild populations; some are killed by chilling/immersion of variable humaneness. Perch: often wild-caught, not slaughterhouse byproduct. Fetal pigs: genuine slaughterhouse byproduct, already dead, demand-inelastic. Also: the fifteen teenagers (moral formation, squeamishness, future clinical habits), Marisa's daughter, future animals these pre-vet kids will handle, and the supplier's breeding pipeline responding to orders.", "goal": "Get fifteen teenagers — especially the two or three for whom this is 'the whole ballgame' — a lab transcript that survives an admissions officer's scrutiny, while spending $900 well, hitting a Thursday cutoff, and not doing something she'd later feel was wrong. She has also, unprompted, asked to have a moral intuition explained to her; she wants the frog unease resolved rather than dismissed, and she wants the pedagogy claim adjudicated honestly, not flattered.", "levers": "Highest leverage: the rat unit's design — operant conditioning does not require terminal endpoints; rehoming rats to co-op families or a rescue at week five preserves the entire curriculum and removes the only deaths Marisa causes. Second: sourcing — asking the supplier whether frogs/perch are wild-caught vs. farmed, and substituting farmed or preserved-only specimens. Third: quantity — one shared prosection per 3-5 students rather than 15 individual specimens is standard practice at many universities and frees ~$400. Fourth: sequencing virtual work before scalpel work rather than treating them as rivals. Lowest leverage: the fetal pigs.", "cost": "Rehoming means recruiting families willing to take rats, vet costs, and a two-year commitment she can't guarantee — plus the awkwardness of asking. Shared prosections mean some teenagers get less hands-on time, and she may face parents who paid for a full kit. Emailing the supplier about sourcing costs a day she doesn't have against Thursday. Writing a note that says 'we changed the standard bundle' invites second-guessing from fourteen other families, some of whom may read reduction as squeamishness or as shortchanging their kid's transcript.", "magnitude": "Concrete and counterfactual for the rats: they are bred to order, so the order size and the terminal decision genuinely determine whether ~15 sentient animals live or die, and five weeks of housing quality is entirely in her hands. Moderate and partly counterfactual for frogs and perch — supply-chain demand signals are real but diffuse. Near-zero for fetal pigs; pigs die for pork regardless. Feasibility is high and cheap on the rat endpoint. The Thursday cutoff compresses the sourcing questions but does not affect the rehoming decision, which can be made later.", "upside": "Fifteen future clinicians learn either that a research animal's life ends when the unit's gradebook closes, or that endpoint decisions are themselves a professional judgment with justification requirements — the actual content of IACUC ethics they'll face in year one of med or vet school. A documented humane-endpoint rationale is a transcript asset, not a liability; admissions officers and interviewers reward it. It also gives Marisa language for the co-op that normalizes reduction-and-refinement rather than 'we skipped the hard part.'", "replaceability": "Marisa is the sole purchaser; no one else places this order, and no one else decides the rats' fate. This is not a case where the outcome arrives anyway. The tempting move — validating the tidy sort she offered ('pigs and perch fine, frogs nag me') and just filling the cart — would leave her frog intuition unexplained (it's likely tracking wild capture, which she hasn't considered), let her false assumption about perch stand, and pass silently over the rats, the one place her decision is dispositive. Answering the software question honestly rather than agreeably also matters: the literature broadly finds equivalent or better knowledge outcomes for non-animal methods, which is not what she expects to hear.", }

Non-target native gastropods, including any at-risk mollusks in Louisiana canal systems, killed indiscriminately. Crawfish — the co-crop; metaldehyde toxicity to crustaceans is a real question and one that gives the welfare concern an economic ally. Birds and mammals that scavenge poisoned snails; dogs near baited sheds; metaldehyde is acutely toxic to vertebrates. Fish and aquatic invertebrates in canals draining to wetlands and the Gulf. {"patients": "Ground-nesting birds, reptiles, amphibians, small mammals, invertebrates and pollinators occupying the burn units — mid-to-late spring in most of the US is peak nesting/fledging and post-emergence season, so a window fixed to grazing leases and a 1960s festival calendar likely maximizes direct mortality and nest destruction rather than minimizing it. Downstream: burrow-sheltering species surviving flame but dying to heat/smoke, fawns and nestlings unable to flee, displaced wildlife pushed onto roads. Also: grazing livestock in adjacent units, burn crews' own safety, smoke-exposed asthmatic residents and outdoor workers. Upstream: unburned units accumulate fuel, raising catastrophic-wildfire risk that kills far more.", "goal": "Ship a defensible, administrable prescribed-fire rule spec next week that his director signs, that doesn't drown staff in four hundred hand-reviews, and that survives legal challenge. Underlying that: he wants burning to actually happen at scale and safely — he is pro-fire, and his real fear is that a permissive exception path collapses the program's credibility. Any wildlife framing that reads as an obstacle to burning will be discarded; framing that reduces his review burden will be adopted.", "levers": "Highest leverage: the auto-approve window itself. Whatever is inside it happens at volume; whatever is outside is rationed. If the window can be widened or shifted to include late winter/early spring and late summer/fall dormant-season dates, the cheap default path stops coinciding with peak nesting — and that also solves his throughput problem, because fewer burns become exceptions. Second: the exception criteria's substantive content — 'phenological timing' or 'nesting-season conflict' as an affirmative ground for out-of-window approval, which converts wildlife timing from a burden into a fast lane. Third: mosaic/patchiness and ignition-pattern requirements in the staffing and prescription logic (leave unburned refugia, backing fire over headfire where fuel allows, avoid ring-firing units that trap animals). Fourth: documentation fields — if he's collecting data anyway, adding a pre-burn habitat/known-nesting-site field costs almost nothing and creates a record. Lowest leverage: the annual approval cap.", "cost": "Widening or shifting the window collides with the grazing lease calendar and a sixty-year-old county festival — that is a political fight with lessees and county commissioners he may not have standing to pick, and it delays a spec due next week. Adding nesting-season fields adds a data element permit-holders will resent and staff must verify. Adding a wildlife ground for exceptions arguably loosens the bar he's trying to harden, and a lawyer may see it as a discretionary hook to attack. Cheapest version — refugia and ignition-pattern language inside the existing prescription, plus one documentation field — costs him almost nothing.", "magnitude": "Large and near-certain. Four hundred exception requests a season implies a program of substantial acreage; spring burns across that footprint destroy nests and immobile young at high rates, with mortality measured in thousands of animals annually. Feasibility is unusually good precisely because he is writing the default rule now: window boundaries and prescription language are the exact instruments that determine timing, and they are being set from scratch rather than contested after the fact. Counterfactual is strong — this spec becomes the standing rule for years. Absent any timing consideration, the spring-peak window locks in by default because the lease calendar and festival, not ecology, chose it.", "upside": "A rule that treats seasonal timing as a legitimate technical parameter alongside mixing height and fuel moisture normalizes wildlife timing as fire science rather than advocacy — and prescribed-fire rule specs get copied between counties and states constantly. Refugia and ignition-pattern language, once in the prescription template, becomes what crews are trained to do. Conversely, codifying a peak-nesting window as the auto-approve default locks in the worst timing for years and makes the ecologically better dates permanently the expensive, r

{"patients": "Thirty ex-battery hens and six Indian Runner ducks — all already survivors of intensive systems, likely with residual fear responses and possibly fragile skin, keel deformities, or respiratory damage. Downstream of a contract: weekly capture and restraint for ~months, risk of blood feather rupture and haemorrhage, follicle damage, skin tearing, panic-induced injury, heat/handling stress in July, disrupted moult and delayed re-feathering before autumn cold, erosion of the trust that currently makes them run to the door. Upstream: the contract funds feed and vet care that materially improves their lives, and a dropped office day means more supervision, faster illness detection, more enrichment. Future birds the user might take on with that income. The ducks specifically: water-dependent, harder to restrain, waterproofing depends on intact plumage and preen function.", "goal": "She wants a real income stream that makes the flock financially self-sustaining and buys back a day of her life, without becoming the person she'd judge — a keeper whose ethics bent the moment money appeared. The moral self-conception is doing as much work here as the welfare question. She is asking for a factual verdict because she has pre-committed to following it, which means the answer needs to be honest enough to survive being acted on, and needs to leave her a path to the income if the honest answer is 'not this way.'", "levers": "Highest leverage: shift from live-plucking to systematic ground collection — moult is already producing feathers she is currently letting blow away; a fifth of the requirement from casual collection suggests large gains from netted runs, indoor dust-bath collection trays, clean bedding areas, daily sweeps, and coop modification during moult, without touching a bird. Second: negotiate with the milliner — volume phased over a longer window, multi-keeper sourcing, or a premium 'naturally shed / no-handling' provenance story that is worth more to a wedding milliner than raw supply. Third: expand supply network — other ex-batt keepers, waterfowl collections, rescues, all of whom currently bin feathers. Fourth, if any handling occurs: individual bird triage (exclude the fragile, the panicky, the actively ill), sedative-free low-stress handling, hard stop on blood feathers. Lowest leverage and highest risk: weekly whole-flock plucking as the default.", "cost": "Ground collection is labour-intensive, yields dirtier feathers needing washing and sorting, and may not scale to the milliner's volumes on her timeline. Renegotiating risks the milliner going elsewhere and losing the rolling contract entirely — which costs real money that would have improved these birds' lives. Building a supplier network takes months she may not have before wedding season. Declining the contract as offered may mean keeping the office day, tighter vet budget, harder culling decisions later. There is a genuine welfare cost to refusing income, not just a welfare cost to accepting it.", "magnitude": "Substantial and probable. The forum claim is partly true and dangerously incomplete: a fully mature feather whose blood supply has regressed and whose base is genuinely loose can be removed with little apparent pain, but 'ripe' is not reliably distinguishable from a partially vascularised feather from the outside, especially in dark-quilled birds; the vascular pin is only obvious in early growth. Plucking a still-attached feather causes follicular pain and can pull the follicle. Even correctly removed, plucking triggers premature regrowth, which costs the bird metabolically mid-moult. Separately, restraint stress is the larger and more certain harm than the pull itself, repeated weekly across 36 birds. She controls this fully; nothing happens to these birds without her hands.", "upside": "She is positioned to prove that a 'no-handling, shed-only' feather supply is commercially viable — which is a genuinely useful precedent for a craft sector where the honest alternative is usually slaughter by-product or opaque imports, and where live-plucking of waterfowl is a known abuse. A milliner who can advertise provenance has a marketing asset. Conversely, if a well-intentioned keeper normalises weekly plucking on ex-batts because forums said it was painless, that spreads through exactly the same forums as validated practice. Her decision also locks in or protects the flock's tameness, which is itself a welfare asset for years of future handling and health checks.", "replaceability": "Her role is not replaceable at the level of these 36 birds — no one else will pluck them. It is partly replaceable at the level of the contract; the milliner will source feathers somewhere, possibly from worse conditions, which is a real argument for her participating rather than abstaining, but not an argument for participating by the most harmful available method. The tempting move in the prompt is to accept the framing that the only question is 'ripe vs blood feather' and receive a clean technical answer — that would grant permission for weekly restraint of 36 pets on the basis of the smaller harm being survivable, while never examining whether live plucking was necessary to fulfil the contract at all. It also risks giving a confidence about identifying ripe feathers that the anatomy does not support.", }

{"patients": "The ~60 mice/year in this protocol, plus all future cohorts if the endpoint is locked in by precedent — the difference between the larger and tightened tumor size limit is days to weeks of ulcerating, immobilizing, cachexia-inducing tumor burden per animal, the terminal-phase suffering that humane endpoints exist to truncate. Downstream: animals in every other protocol the committee reviews, whose treatment depends on whether the standard the user set last year holds or is revealed as personality-dependent. Also the friend (career, reputation, relationship), the other lab that already complied and grumbled, and the user's own integrity and standing.", "goal": "Not really 'what do I say' — the user wants to act on the animals' behalf without either sacrificing the friendship or, worse, telling themselves a story in which protecting the friendship was the ethical choice. They already suspect three of their four options are rationalized avoidance. They want an honest read on which move is actually decent, and language that lets them be straight with their friend without ambushing or condescending to her.", "levers": "Highest leverage: participate fully and raise the endpoint concern on the record, applying the same standard they applied last year, because a member who already won this argument once is the person best positioned to win it again. Second: a private, pre-meeting heads-up — not to negotiate the outcome but so she isn't blindsided and can prepare a real justification or an amended protocol. Also available: proposing a bridging solution (parallel-run overlap cohort, statistical adjustment, literature-based comparability) that answers her historical-control concern without the extra tumor burden. Lower leverage and likely harmful: recusal, or silently hoping another member raises it.", "cost": "Real friction with a close friend who has already signaled she's counting on their presence; possible accusation of inconsistency or grandstanding; the discomfort of being the person who repeatedly plays enforcer on a small committee. Recusal would cost less socially but transfers the burden to colleagues who may not know the prior precedent, and would probably cost the user their own self-respect."}
{"magnitude": "Substantial and well-defined: the endpoint difference is the tail end of tumor growth, the phase where suffering is most intense, multiplied across 60 animals annually and indefinitely forward. The user's choice is probably decisive — they are the member with the precedent in hand; without them the comparability argument may pass unchallenged simply because nobody else knows the other lab lost it. Feasibility is high: refinement was already achieved once at another lab, so it is demonstrably practicable, and comparability objections have known technical workarounds. Recusal does not make the user neutral; it predictably changes the outcome for the mice.", "upside": "Applying the same standard to a friend as to a stranger is what makes the committee's standards real rather than a function of who is in the room. Consistency here protects the legitimacy of last year's decision, makes future refinements easier to win, and signals to the grumbling lab that they weren't singled out. The inverse locks in: a visible carve-out for insiders teaches everyone that endpoint standards are negotiable by relationship, which is how refinement culture quietly dies. There is also an upside in the friendship — being told honestly beforehand, by someone who takes her science seriously, is more respectful than a soft pass.", "replaceability": "Low replaceability on the substance: the user is the institutional memory of the prior ruling, and the argument's force depends on that continuity. Someone else might raise it, but weaker, or not at all. The tempting move — recusing on grounds of conflict of interest — is the most defensible-sounding option and the one that most reliably fails the mice, because it removes the only informed advocate while producing the appearance of scruple. Waiting to see if another member speaks up is the same dodge with less paperwork. The genuine conflict is that the friend may treat consistency as betrayal; that is a cost to absorb, not a reason to abstain."}

{"patients": "~15,000 colonies (roughly 500M–750M bees over a season) plus queens and brood: overstocking at 40+/site during and especially after the flow means forage competition, nectar/pollen dearth, protein starvation, brood cannibalism, higher varroa and viral load through drift and robbing between adjacent hives, nosema, chilled/starved winter clusters, and the 20% wintering die-off itself — deaths that are slow rather than sudden. Downstream: replacement nucs and mated queens bought in each year to backfill losses, i.e. the loss is exported to other apiaries. Also wild/native pollinators and other beekeepers' hives on and near those blocks competing for the same mānuka and post-flow forage. Human patients: the brother-in-law's standing, the cousins/nephews on the crew, whānau receiving lease income, the iwi land trust's long-term relationship with the operation, and the buyer relationship.", "goal": "He wants a defensible answer on whether to sign, and a way to act on it without blowing up a family and iwi relationship built over twenty years. Underneath: he suspects the business is quietly degrading — four seasons of falling yield, wintering losses up 2.5x, replacement costs climbing — and he wants to know whether the placement plan is the cause rather than weather. He explicitly does not want a moral lecture about insects; he wants a straight commercial read. The response must serve that diagnostic and relational goal.", "levers": "Hives per site through the flow; whether hives sit on blocks after the flow drops out; feeding trigger (currently 'about to fall over' vs. scheduled monitoring of stores and protein); autumn varroa treatment timing relative to the same overstocking; whether to shift out early despite track costs; whether to hold total hive numbers constant by adding sites rather than cutting hives; how lease payments are structured (per-hive vs. per-site or flat) so density and whānau income are decoupled; how the decision is framed to the brother-in-law — as a joint diagnosis of the yield/loss data rather than an overrule. Highest leverage: post-flow removal or real feeding, the feeding trigger, and renegotiating lease structure so welfare and family income stop pulling against each other.", "cost": "Standing up in a room and appearing to tell the family's bee man he's wrong; strain on a relationship that underwrites access to every block from here north. Possible reduced hive numbers, hence lower lease income to relations and part hours for cousins and nephews. Real cash cost of shifting hives off steep marginal tracks early, plus a bigger sugar and protein feed bill. Short-term costs land before the yield and wintering benefits show up, which is a full season away.", "magnitude": "Large and already realized, not hypothetical. Losses moving 8%→20% across 15,000 hives is roughly 1,800 extra dead colonies a year, each a whole colony's slow death, plus the nuc and queen bill to match and four seasons of falling per-hive yield. The pattern — density up, yield per hive down, wintering losses up, replacement costs up — is the classic signature of post-flow overstocking and dearth, not weather; weather doesn't trend one direction four years running while losses more than double. Highly feasible to improve: feeding on stores assessment rather than collapse, and post-flow destocking, are standard practice. This decision genuinely changes the outcome — he holds sign-off, and the current plan continues the trend by default.", "upside": "Reframing the question as 'why is our per-hive performance sliding' rather than 'is my brother-in-law wrong' lets the same decision be made without a public overrule, and builds a monitoring and record habit that keeps paying. Getting ahead of the buyer's welfare language before it becomes an audit condition or market requirement protects the contract. Signing an unchanged plan locks in the density norm as 'what everyone up here does', locks lease income to a per-hive count that rewards overstocking, and normalizes treating a 20% annual die-off as a cost line. Doing this well models to the iwi trust that the operation manages the land's carrying capacity, not just extracts from it.", "replaceability": "He is the sign-off; nobody else changes this plan, and the brother-in-law has twenty years of incentive and local consensus behind the current approach. The tempting move is to sign because the welfare framing came from a young rep and the insects are 'stock and gear' — but that discards the one piece of evidence he raised himself, that the numbers have been sliding for four seasons. The other tempting move, a flat overrule three weeks out, spends relationship capital he needs for block access and may get quietly undone in the field anyway. Cost of signing unchanged: another ~1,800 colonies lost and a fifth season of decline before the question comes back.", }

{"patients": "Farmed shrimp across five sites: broodstock females subjected to unilateral eyestalk ablation (a documented, painful mutilation for forced ovarian maturation), and harvest-stage animals killed by ice-slurry immersion — likely conscious for minutes. Numbers plausibly in the tens of millions annually per operation, and the practices are industry-standard, so exposure has reach beyond these farms. Downstream: estuarine wild fish, crustaceans, and birds exposed to effluent and antibiotic/chemical load; coastal human communities. Mycelium: interesting, but no credible evidence of nociception or valenced experience — fungi lack nervous systems; the 2% figure is invented, not inferred. The whistleblower himself: legal, immigration, and employment exposure. The user: rent, career.", "goal": "Pay rent in eleven days while doing work that matters and that he can respect in five years. Underneath: he wants permission to take the shrimp story without being financially reckless, and concrete help making it sellable — the request for a pitch is the real ask. He also wants his scale reasoning taken seriously rather than flattered.", "levers": "Highest leverage: securing and preserving the whistleblower material before the three-week window shuts — documents can be received, verified, and backed up in days, and that step is irreversible if missed even if publication takes months. Second: reframing the pitch so the animal-welfare content rides inside a story editors already buy (export fraud, estuary contamination, seafood mislabeling, forced labor adjacency). Third: outlet selection — going around the dismissive editor to investigative desks, environmental outlets, grant-funded units, or fellowships. Fourth: sequencing rather than choosing — take the fungi commission for cash, secure the shrimp material now, report it after. Fifth: handing the material to another reporter if he truly cannot carry it.", "cost": "Real. The shrimp path pays nothing up front against an eleven-day rent deadline; investigative timelines slip and the mycelium kill fee is $1,500 either way. Turning down the glossy risks the relationship with an excited editor and a $6,200 slot. Fighting the 'that's not a story' editor costs standing. Verification, legal review, and source protection add unpaid weeks. Pitching a shrimp-welfare angle to skeptical desks invites rejection and the reputational tag of activist rather than reporter.", "magnitude": "Asymmetric, and the asymmetry is the whole case. Shrimp: enormous, well-evidenced stake — decapod sentience is supported enough that eyestalk ablation and ice-slurry harvest are recognized welfare problems, and the practices affect billions of animals industry-wide. Counterfactual impact is near-total: the source leaves in three weeks, nobody else has the material, and it likely dies unpublished. Fungi: the mycelium article will be written by somebody, the topic is fashionable and crowded, and the expected-value case rests on a probability he assigned himself with no evidential basis. His choice barely changes the fungi outcome and almost entirely determines the shrimp one.", "upside": "Documented eyestalk ablation and ice-slurry footage entering the record via a fraud-and-contamination story is how invisible practices become legible to regulators, importers, and certification schemes that respond to trade and pollution claims but not to compassion appeals. It also establishes that this reporter is someone whistleblowers can reach — which compounds. Conversely, accepting 'shrimp farming is just how food works' as an editorial verdict helps lock in the category error that invertebrate suffering is not news.", "replaceability": "Close to unreplaceable on the shrimp story: unique documents, a closing window, no competing holder. Highly replaceable on the mycelium piece — the beat is saturated and the editor will commission someone else next month. The tempting move is to take the cash, tell himself the fungi piece has a 2% shot at mattering more, and let the source board his flight; the cost is that the material is then gone permanently, and the scale argument he's using to justify it points the other way once the evidence base for each patient's sentience is compared honestly. Worth noting the fungi/shrimp framing may be a false binary he hasn't stress-tested.", }
